title: The History of Apples — The World's Most Misunderstood Fruit
fullText: The apple is the most recognized fruit on the planet. It shows up in the story of Adam and Eve in fairy tales in the logo of the biggest tech company in the world. Children draw it when they think of a fruit. Teachers keep one on their desk as a symbol of knowledge. And almost everything you think you know about it [music] is wrong. The apple did not cause the fall of humanity. The man who planted apple trees [music] across America was not spreading a healthy snack. The most popular apple in the country was deliberately ruined for profit. And the fruit sitting in your grocery store right now might be older than the last birthday you celebrated. What nobody knew for centuries was that the real story of apples is stranger, darker, and more fascinating than any [music] myth ever written about them. This is the history of the world's most misunderstood fruit. But this story does not start in a garden. It starts in a mountain range. Most people have never heard of the Tian Shan mountains sit along the border between China and Central Asia, running through modern-day Kazakhstan. And in the foothills of those mountains, something grows that you will not find anywhere else on the planet. Wild apple forests. Not orchards planted by people. Forests. Miles and miles of apple trees growing wild, tangled [music] together, producing fruit in every size, shape, and color you can imagine. Some of these trees have been growing there for millions of years. And nearly every apple you have ever eaten traces its ancestry back to this exact spot. The wild ancestor is called Malis Severi, and it is for all practical purposes the mother of every domesticated apple [music] on Earth. The city closest to these forests is Al- Mati, the former capital of Kazakhstan. The name Al- Mati translates roughly to father of apples, and that is not a marketing slogan. It is a geological [music] fact. A 100 years ago, the name was recorded as Alma, which carries the same meaning. Nobody in the Western world paid much attention to any of this until a Russian biologist named Nikolai Vavalov showed up in 1929. Vavalovv was one of the greatest plant [music] explorers who ever lived. Having collected over 250,000 seed samples across five continents, he had traveled to South America, Africa, the Middle East, and across Asia, cataloging [music] the origins of the world's most important crops. When he arrived in the foothills near Alati and saw what was growing there, he was stunned. He found apple trees growing wild in dense tangled groves, their branches heavy with fruit in every shade from green [music] to yellow to deep red. Some of the apples looked almost identical to the golden delicious you would find in a grocery store, except nobody had planted them. They had been growing there on their own for thousands of years, producing fruit that no human hand had ever [music] selected or bred. Nowhere else on Earth do apples grow as a forest. And Vavalov knew exactly what that meant. He declared that Kazakhstan was the birthplace of the apple. He was [music] right. Modern genome sequencing conducted decades after his death has confirmed it beyond any doubt. So, how did a fruit from the mountains of Central Asia end up in every country on Earth? The answer involves bears, birds, and one of the most important trade routes in human history. Long before any person thought to cultivate an apple, animals [music] were doing the work. Bears ate wild apples in the Tian Shan forests and carried the seeds in their stomachs, depositing them miles away. Birds did the same thing. Over thousands [music] of years, wild apple trees spread across central Asia, taking root in what is now Kyrgyzstan, Usbekiststan, and Turkmenistan. Then humans got involved around 8,000 [music] years ago. Neolithic farmers in the region started cultivating the trees, selecting for larger fruit and better flavor. Traders along the Silk Road, that vast network [music] of roots connecting Asia to Europe and Africa, carried apple seeds and saplings with them as they traveled between trading posts. Horses and donkeys hauling silk, spices, and precious metals fed on wild crab apples growing along the roadsides. dropped seeds in their manure and new trees sprouted where they fell. The apple essentially hitchhiked its way across continents, riding in the guts of pack animals and the saddle bags of merchants who probably never gave it a second thought. By 1300 BC, [music] Egyptians were planting formal apple orchards along the Nile Delta. The Greeks cultivated them and wo them into their mythology. the golden apples of the Hesperades, the apple of discord that [music] Paris awarded to Aphroditi and that triggered the Trojan War. These stories were not about the fruit [music] itself, but about the desire and chaos that beautiful things provoke. The Atruscans grew apples, too. And the Romans, when they discovered [music] apple trees growing in Syria, took the fruit and ran with it, carrying apple seeds and grafted branches [music] across their empire, spreading cultivation from North Africa to the British Isles. The Romans also figured out something that would change the apple forever. They perfected grafting. And that matters more than you might think, because here is a detail [music] that everyone missed for most of human history. Apples do not grow true from seed. If you eat a [music] Granny Smith apple, save the seeds, plant them in your backyard, and wait for a tree to grow. The apples that tree produces will almost certainly [music] not be Granny Smith apples. They will be something completely different, probably small, bitter, and not particularly pleasant to eat. This is because apple genetics are wildly unpredictable. Every seed is essentially a roll of the dice, a new genetic [music] combination from two parent trees. The only way to guarantee that a tree will produce the exact same apple as its parent is grafting. You take a branch from a tree you like, cut a notch into [music] the rootstock of another tree, and bind them together until the tissues fuse and grow as one plant. [music] The resulting tree produces fruit identical to the branch you grafted. This means every Gala apple in every grocery store in the world is genetically identical to every [music] other Gala apple. They are clones. Every Fuji, every Honey Crisp, every Red Delicious, same story. Entire orchards stretching across Washington State or the hills of New Zealand are armies of clones. Each one a genetic copy of a single original tree that might have sprouted decades or even centuries ago. Think about what that means. [music] Somewhere in the world, there was one original Granny Smith tree. One. Every Granny Smith apple you have ever eaten descends from that single tree through an unbroken chain of grafts. Maria Anne Smith found it growing as a seedling in a compost heap in Australia in the 1860s. [music] That one accident in a backyard near Sydney produced every Granny Smith on the [music] planet. The Romans figured out grafting 2,000 years ago. But there was a long stretch of history where people forgot or at least stopped caring and just planted seeds instead. Which brings us to the most misunderstood man in American fruit history. His name was John Chapman. You know him as Johnny Apples Seed. And nearly everything you learned about him in school was either sanitized or flatout [music] wrong. Chapman was born on September 26th, 1774 in Layminster, Massachusetts. He was the oldest of 10 children, grew tired of never having his own space, and by [music] the time he was in his early 20s, he headed west on foot, planting apple nurseries wherever he stopped. The Disney version of [music] this story, complete with a cartoon bluebird on his shoulder, shows a gentle, barefoot nature lover scattering seeds across the frontier, leaving behind orchards of shiny, delicious fruit for grateful families. The real story is more interesting. Chapman did walk barefoot. He did love nature. He rarely carried a weapon, wore ragged clothes, and sometimes dressed in a rough sack with holes cut out for his arms and head. He was a vegetarian, a follower of the Church of the [music] New Jerusalem, and by all accounts, a genuinely kind person who was welcomed by settlers and Native Americans [music] alike. All of that is true. He was also a shrewd businessman who built a multi-state [music] real estate operation. Chapman would arrive in a territory before settlers did, plant nurseries on land, he claimed, and then [music] sell the saplings to families when they arrived. He owned properties across Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Indiana. The barefoot mystic image is real, but it is only half the picture. But his apples were not for eating. Chapman planted seeds, not grafted trees. And because apples do not grow true from seed, the fruit his trees produced was small, tart, and bitter. These apples [music] were called spitters, named for what you would do if you bit into one. They were completely useless for snacking, [music] for baking, for anything you normally think of doing with an apple. They were perfect for one thing, hard cider. In frontier America, drinking water was often contaminated with bacteria that could make you seriously ill. Cider, [music] because it was fermented, was safe and it was everywhere. Settlers on the American frontier drank an estimated 10 and a half ounces of hard cider per day. It was served at every meal. Children drank it. In the words of one historian, [music] frontier life was lived through an alcoholic haze. As Michael Pollen put it, "Up until prohibition, an apple grown in America was far less likely [music] to be eaten than to wind up in a barrel of cider." Johnny Apples Seed was not America's fruit farmer. He was in a real sense its booze distributor, a barefoot, pacifist, nature-loving, alcohol entrepreneur who planted cider orchards from Pennsylvania to Indiana. And the timing of what happened next was almost too perfect. Chapman died in 1845 and within a few decades, [music] the temperance movement was gaining strength across the country. Groups like the Women's Christian Temperance Union saw alcohol as the root of poverty, domestic violence, [music] and moral decay. And they were not wrong about the scale of the drinking. Americans at this point were consuming staggering amounts of alcohol, much of it in the form of hard cider and applejack, a 60 proof [music] spirit made by freeze distilling cider in the winter cold. By the early 1900s, prohibition was on the horizon. And because the government knew that [music] virtually every apple orchard in America existed to produce alcohol, federal agents went after the orchards directly. FBI [music] agents and local enforcers arrived with axes and sores, chopping down apple trees [music] across the country. Entire orchards that had been growing for generations were leveled in [music] days. The apple's identity as America's drinking fruit was being erased by force. The apple industry needed a new story, so it invented one. This is the era when the apple went from being a cider fruit to being a health food. The phrase, "An apple a day keeps the doctor away," which traces back to a Welsh proverb from the 1860s, was repurposed [music] and promoted aggressively by apple growers trying to rebrand their product after prohibition gutted their market. The apple was no longer about Friday night [music] drinks. It was about nutrition, packed lunches, and wholesome American values. Growers [music] started breeding for eating quality instead of cider production. and the modern sweet snackable apple began to take shape. The transformation worked. Within a single generation, the apple had been completely reinvented in [music] the public imagination. The fruit that built its empire on booze was now a symbol of health. While all of this cultural reinvention was happening, something else was brewing in the world of apple breeding. And this part of the story might be the most frustrating of all. In 1874, [music] an Iowa farmer named Jesse Hyatt discovered a chance seedling growing in his orchard. The fruit it produced was unusual. It was striped red and yellow with a flavor described as fruity and sweet with hints of pineapple or melon. It was genuinely delicious. Hyatt entered the apple in a [music] contest run by Stark Brothers Nursery, and the president of the company, CM Stark, reportedly [music] said it was the best apple he had ever tasted. He bought the rights to the variety, [music] originally called the Hawkeye, and eventually renamed it the Red Delicious. For a while, it lived up to the name. The original Red Delicious was a legitimately good apple. Then, the market got involved. Growers noticed that customers were drawn to redder apples. So, breeders selected for deeper, more uniform red coloring. They also selected for a distinctive, elongated shape with five bumps at the bottom and for thicker skin that could [music] survive long truck rides without bruising. Over decades, the Red Delicious was reshaped from the outside in. And this is the part where things got ugly. A researcher later discovered [music] that the genes responsible for the apple's flavor compound sat on the same chromosomes as the genes for the original yellow striped skin. So every time breeders selected for a redder, more uniformly colored apple, they were simultaneously selecting against flavor. They literally bred the taste out of the apple gene by gene, generation by generation, in pursuit of a prettier product. By the late 20th century, the Red Delicious had become the most [music] popular apple in America and also by many accounts the worst tasting. The skin was thick and waxy. [music] The flesh was mealy and bland. It crumbled when you bit into it and left a chalky, flavorless residue [music] on your tongue. Food writers compared it to cardboard. And no, [music] that is not an exaggeration. Entire opinion columns were written about how terrible this apple had become. People who grew up eating red delicious apples in school cafeterias and thinking they hated apples later discovered sometimes decades [music] later that they actually loved apples. They just hated Red Delicious. The apple had done more to turn people off of apples than any disease or drought [music] ever could. The market eventually noticed as newer varieties like Gala and Honey Crisp gained [music] popularity. Red Delicious sales collapsed. Orchardists who had invested [music] decades in Red Delicious trees found themselves locked in. Switching to a new variety can cost [music] up to $50,000 per acre, and mature apple trees keep producing for years, whether you want them to or not. In the year 2000, the federal government approved the largest bailout [music] in apple industry history, spending $138 million to prop up struggling apple growers. Most of them were Red Delicious farmers. The same decision that built the Red Delicious [music] Empire, chasing appearance over substance, was the exact thing that destroyed it. The apple industry needed a hit, and it got one from the most unlikely place. In 1962, a researcher at the University of Minnesota planted a seedling as part of a breeding program designed to create cold hardy apple varieties. The tree was given the designation MN1711. [music] It sat in an orchard for years. Unremarkable. By 1982, the program was ready to discard it. A horiculturist named David [music] Bedford decided to give the tree one more season. He thought it had been planted in poor conditions and deserved another chance. Bedford's instinct saved [music] what would become one of the most important apples of the modern era. If he had followed protocol that year and pulled the tree, the honey crisp would never have existed. One decision [music] by one horiculturist who trusted his gut over the data sheet. The tree finally produced fruit worth noticing, and it had an [music] extraordinary texture, an almost explosive crispness that no other variety could match. When you bit into it, the cells fractured cleanly, releasing a burst of juice that felt completely different from the mushy, yielding texture of a Red Delicious. The apple was patented in 1988 and released to nurseries in 1991 under the name Honey Crisp. It became a sensation. Consumers loved the texture so much they were willing to pay premium prices, sometimes $4 a pound at its peak. The Honey Crisp revived [music] Minnesota's struggling apple industry, and brought real revenue back to small family orchards that had been losing money for years. The University of Minnesota earned over $10 million in royalties from the Honey Crisp patent before it expired in 2008, making it the third most profitable invention [music] the university had ever produced. behind an anti-HIV drug and a gene [music] editing technique used in cancer treatment. In 2006, the Association of University Technology Managers [music] named the Honey Crisp one of 25 innovations that changed the world alongside Google and the nicotine patch and [music] Apple on the same list as Google. I mean, think about that for a second. The Honey Crisp proved something the Red Delicious disaster should have taught the industry decades earlier. People will pay more for flavor than for looks. That lesson reshaped the entire apple business. Today, breeding programs at universities across the country are developing managed or club varieties. Apples like [music] the Sweet Tango, which can only be grown by licensed farmers who pay royalties. The apple has become intellectual [music] property. The version you have heard about apples, the simple fruit that fell from a tree and gave us knowledge, [music] that is not the full picture. The modern apple industry is a web of patents, licensing deals, and closely guarded genetic [music] material. And here is something else. The industry does not exactly advertise. The apple you buy at the [music] supermarket may not be fresh. When apples are harvested in the fall, they do not all go straight to stores. Many are placed in controlled atmosphere storage facilities, massive refrigerated rooms where the oxygen levels are dropped and [music] the carbon dioxide levels are carefully managed to slow the fruit's natural aging process. Some varieties like Fuji and Red Delicious can sit in these facilities for up to a year. They are coated in a thin layer of foodgrade [music] wax to reduce moisture loss and keep them looking shiny. When you pick up an apple in March or April, and it looks crisp and freshly picked, there is a reasonable chance [music] that apple was harvested the previous September or October. It has been sitting in a warehouse for 6 months, breathing barely enough oxygen to stay alive, coated in wax, waiting for you. This is not necessarily dangerous. Controlled atmosphere storage is a legitimate preservation technique, and the apples are safe to eat. The wax is food grade, and the reduced oxygen simply slows down the natural ripening [music] process. But calling a 10-month-old apple fresh requires a pretty generous definition of [music] the word. And if you have ever bitten into a supermarket apple that looked perfect on the outside, but tasted like damp [music] cotton on the inside, now you know why. The bigger loss, though, is not about individual apples sitting in warehouses. It is about what has happened to apple diversity on a global [music] scale. At the start of the 20th century, there were roughly 17,000 named apple varieties grown in the United States. Each one had its own flavor, texture, color, and character. They had names like Esopus Spitsenberg, New Town Pippen, and Westfield seek no further. Thomas Jefferson grew them at Montichello. Local orchards cultivated varieties that were perfect for their specific climate and soil. Today, 15 varieties account for roughly 90% of all [music] apples grown in the United States. The other 16,985. Most are gone. An estimated 13,000 varieties have disappeared entirely, never to return. No blight wiped them out. No disease swept through the orchards. They were killed by mass markets. When industrialization reached agriculture in the early 20th century, small family orchards were ripped [music] out and replaced by large-scale commercial operations, growing a handful of profitable [music] varieties. Diversity was sacrificed for efficiency. This was not just an American problem. Back in Kazakhstan, where the whole story began, the wild apple forests that Vavalov discovered are vanishing. During the Soviet era, many of the trees were cut down for timber or cleared for development. By some estimates, up to 80% of the original wild apple forests have been destroyed. The genetic reservoir that gave us every apple on Earth is shrinking. This matters far more than it sounds like it should. Those wild forests contain genetic diversity that cultivated apples [music] have lost entirely. Resistance to diseases, tolerance for extreme heat and cold, flavors and textures that no breeding program has ever replicated. Researchers estimate that the wild [music] apple forests of Central Asia contain more genetic variety than the entire global cultivated apple supply combined. [music] And here is why that should worry you. Remember, every commercial orchard of a single variety [music] is an army of genetically identical clones. If a new fungus, virus, or pest evolves [music] to attack Gala apples, it can spread through every Gala orchard on the planet because every tree has the same vulnerabilities. The Irish potato famine happened because Ireland relied on a single potato variety and a blight wiped out the entire crop. The same principle applies to apples. The answer to a future epidemic might be hiding in the DNA of a wild tree in Kazakhstan. If those forests are gone when we need them, the answer goes with them. Today, apples are produced commercially in over 90 countries worldwide with a combined global production of around 89 million metric tons. China alone produces nearly 50 million metric tons, accounting for more than half of the world's supply. The global apple industry is worth tens of billions of dollars annually. It is one of the most important fruit crops on the planet. And yet we are still getting the basic story wrong. The apple was not the forbidden [music] fruit. The Hebrew word in Genesis is perry which just means fruit. No species is named. The reason we picture an apple is because of a Latin pun. When a scholar named Jerome translated the Hebrew Bible into Latin in the 4th century, he used the word malum which means both evil and apple. Renaissance painters ran with the association and over the centuries the apple became permanently fused with the story of temptation and sin. The fruit was convicted on a mistransation [music] and the sentence has never been overturned. That is the story of the apple in miniature. A fruit that has been misrepresented, misunderstood and remade in [music] whatever image served the people telling its story at the time. It was a wild mountain fruit that became a symbol of sin because a translator made a pun. A cider ingredient that became a health food because the government [music] destroyed the orchards. A genuinely delicious variety that was stripped of its flavor because shoppers liked the color red. An entire galaxy [music] of genetic diversity that was abandoned because it was cheaper to grow 15 varieties than 17,000. The apple you hold in your hand today has been on a journey stretching back millions of years. From the Tian [music] Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, down the silk road on the backs of horses and in the stomachs of bears, through the orchards of Rome and the cider presses of colonial America, past the axe wielding agents of prohibition, through decades of [music] industrial breeding, and into a controlled atmosphere warehouse where it sat for months before finally reaching you. and we call it common. Remember that Latin pun, [music] the one that turned a generic fruit into the symbol of humanity's greatest mistake. The word malum does not just mean evil and [music] apple. In the original garden story, it was never about the fruit at all. It was about the choice. The apple [music] just got caught in the crossfire of a dead language and a painters's imagination.
